A sérült felkutatását és mentését azonnal megkezdte az Országos Mentőszolgálat rétsági egysége, a Nógrád Vármegyei Katasztrófavédelmi Igazgatóság rétsági hivatásos tűzoltói, Szokolyáról a Börzsönyi Hegyimentő Szolgálat, valamint egy terepjáró gépkocsival az Ipoly-völgyi Különleges Mentők . A helyszínen az egészségügyi szakemberek fájdalomcsillapítás mellett ellátták a sérültet és rögzítették a sérült végtagot. Photograph: Óscar del Pozo/AFP/Getty Images Spain Spain’s trust in high-speed rail ‘broken’ after second deadly crash this year, says PM Pedro Sánchez vows to investigate crash that killed 69 people – and rebuild public confidence Europe live – latest updates Sam Jones in Madrid and Jakub Krupa Fri 30 Oct 2026 10.13 EDT Last modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 11.14 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has admitted “trust in high-speed rail has been broken” after Wednesday’s train collision that killed at least 69 people, injured more than 100 and prompted a national debate on the safety of the country’s rail network. Sánchez said Spain was “working tirelessly” to provide information as quickly as possible to the families of the victims – who include people from at least 23 different foreign countries – adding his government was committed to finding what had caused the country’s second deadly train collision this year. Two trains, one from Spain’s state-owned Renfe and the other from the private rail company Iryo, were travelling from Madrid towards the southern region of Andalucía on Wednesday when they collided just before 9am . After the Iryo train came to a halt, the other train slammed into its rear , knocking several carriages off the track near Urda, in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha. 10:20 Survivors shell-shocked after deadly Spain train crash - The Latest The crash came nine months after 46 people were killed and dozens injured when two trains – again one from Renfe and one from Iryo – collided on the same line near the town of Adamuz, in Andalucía. “It’s unacceptable for a country like Spain – which has such a powerful high-speed rail system – to experience two accidents of this nature and magnitude within a single year,” the prime minister said on Friday. “Therefore, our task isn’t merely to investigate the causes of what occurred, but also to provide solutions to further strengthen our nation’s high-speed rail system. Public trust in the high-speed system has been broken; the government’s responsibility goes beyond diagnosing the causes – it must also offer solutions to ensure that a tragedy of this scale doesn’t happen again.” View image in fullscreen Pedro Sánchez (L) and the Castilla-La Mancha regional president Emiliano Garcia Page hold a press conference. Photograph: Angeles Visdomine/EPA Shortly after Sánchez spoke, Spain’s transport minister, Óscar Puente, who is under growing pressure to resign, gave a press conference in which he dismissed calls to step down, promising instead to focus on “providing the Spanish people with solutions” to restore trust. “My duty now isn’t to talk about whether or not I carry on with my job; it’s to solve the problems, clarify what happened and offer clear explanations,” he said. “The most important thing I can do is offer solutions as best I can. If the investigation shows there were failures of organisation or control, we will act accordingly. And if individuals are found to be responsible, action will be taken.” Puente once again suggested that responsibility for Wednesday’s crash appeared to lie within the Madrid control centre of Spain’s state infrastructure operator, Adif. He said that in the run-up to the crash, the LZB signalling system – which automatically halts a train if the line ahead is occupied – had gone down, but emphasised that such incidents were not uncommon. Once the system was down, he said, control and decision-making powers reverted to humans, as was the case in other transport sectors. The minister added that the crash had occurred after an Adif operator ordered the Renfe train to move off at “normal” speed, rather than following the protocols, which stipulate a top speed of 40kph (25mph) so that drivers can see any dangers ahead in good time. According to a preliminary investigation report released on Thursday, the Renfe train was travelling at between 160kph and 200kph when it hit the Iryo train. The report concluded: “The sequence of malfunctions, instructions, and actions eventually led to the collision, in the absence of the necessary mitigating barriers.” Puente said the operator in question was a 48-year-old man , with all the relevant up-to-date training and two years of experience in control centres, who had been managing this specific area since February this year. “So, it was a sector he knew well,” the minister added. Transport unions have pushed back at the government, arguing that current workloads are too demanding to handle safely and asking for more personnel. “We believe [the minister] is blaming a mere worker who was working under increasingly poor conditions,” Raquel Ayllón, a spokesperson for SCF, Spain’s railway traffic controllers union, told the Associated Press. “Human error isn’t incomprehensible. What is incomprehensible is that the safety system is regularly failing.” Spain’s conservative People’s party (PP), which is forecast to topple Sánchez’ socialist-led minority coalition government in next month’s snap general election, has repeatedly called for Puente to step down. The PP’s leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, said his party was holding Puente and Sánchez “politically responsible” for both rail crashes. “Whoever has failed in their duty to run the transport ministry properly must bear the consequences,” he said. “And the person who appointed them – and kept them in their post – even more so. If they do not resign, we will remove them at the ballot box.” Ada Colau, the former Barcelona mayor who now leads the leftwing Frente Amplio coalition that is running in the election, also said Puente needed to go. “We’re not going to engage in the triviality of debating whether that resignation should take place today, tomorrow, or the day after,” she said. “It must happen as soon as possible.” Puente, asked about the possible effect of the latest crash on the election , said he had given the matter “zero thought”. “I don’t believe anyone would expect me to be thinking about the election campaign at a moment like this,” he told reporters. https://www.wsws.org/en/articles/2026/11.text: Menu Search Latest Profile English Contact | About | International Committee of the Fourth International ( ICFI ) Menu Search International Committee of the Fourth International ( ICFI ) Latest Profile Fourth International Socialist Equality Party IYSSE About the WSWS Contact Donate On Saturday afternoon, Michał O. drove his car onto the Main Market Square in Kraków and opened fire indiscriminately on civilians from inside the vehicle. According to the latest information, he killed six people, including one British citizen, and injured another 16, some of them critically. Among the injured were two police officers who managed to arrest him after a car chase and a brief exchange of gunfire. The authorities appealed for blood donations. An amateur video posted online shows the attacker shooting at two police officers lying on the ground. [Photo by X] The 24-year-old Polish attacker was also seriously injured. He underwent two operations and died in hospital on Monday morning. He was wearing military camouflage clothing, a helmet and a protective vest and “used a military-style rifle,” according to the Krakow police spokesperson. The weapon was apparently a semi-automatic AR-15 assault rifle, for which the perpetrator held an official firearms licence. Additional weapons and ammunition were found in his vehicle. According to Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, the attacker was not a member of the Polish armed forces. At the attacker’s home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, approximately two hours’ drive to the north, police later discovered the bodies of his parents and sister. According to local authorities, they died on Saturday morning. All three bodies had gunshot wounds. Like his father, the perpetrator was a sport shooter, and the family owned several firearms, a fact known in the neighbourhood. The family had lived in the rented house for more than ten years and was regarded as an ordinary, friendly family. Michał himself was considered quiet and withdrawn, but nevertheless helpful. According to Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski, the perpetrator is believed to have held “very radical views.” Investigators found “indications that he espoused a far-right ideology” in the apartment. Whether and how this was connected to the crime remains unclear. What is clear, at the very least, is that his martial combat gear suggests roots in a militaristic, gun-oriented culture. At the same time, contradictory claims are circulating on social media about his alleged sympathies for Russia or Ukraine, for fascists or for the LGBTQ movement. On Sunday, prosecutor Tomasz Waszczuk, spokesperson for the Krakow District Prosecutor’s Office investigating the case, announced that the attack was being classified as an act of terrorism. President Karol Nawrocki has declared two days of national mourning. The attack in Poland’s second-largest city took place shortly before Independence Day on November 11. Although the circumstances surrounding the crime remain unclear, it is certainly the largest attack since the restoration of capitalism in 1990. In recent decades, Poland has experienced neither major mass shootings nor terrorist attacks of the kind that have tragically become commonplace in other countries. Poland’s crime rate is comparatively low, and its homicide rate per capita is below the EU average. Right-wing politicians have repeatedly cited this as evidence of the success of strict laws and restrictive immigration policies. In fact, however, the only attack that caused a shock comparable to the latest incident was the assassination of the liberal mayor of Gdańsk in 2019. Paul Adamowicz was stabbed to death on stage during a charity concert by a 28-year-old supporter of the Law and Justice party (PiS). Adamowicz was one of the fiercest critics of the then PiS government. Violent attacks in Polish schools have been rare and, due to strict gun laws, have generally involved blunt-force injuries and stabbings. But this appears to be becoming a thing of the past. One indication is the increase in firearms licences by 50,000 to 411,000 in 2025 alone. Violence is rising particularly in schools. At the beginning of October, a corresponding wave of violence shook Poland’s schools. Within three days, one person was murdered and around two dozen injured. The nervousness of the authorities was evident in their decision to conduct bag searches at more than 80,000 schools within just a few days and arrest 135 people, particularly over threats made online. Behind such individual incidents lie more fundamental social developments. In 2023, following mass shootings in California, the WSWS wrote: “Mass shootings, however, cannot simply be explained by individual motives. Mass violence is a social phenomenon and therefore also requires an understanding of social issues.” In Poland, alongside sharply intensifying class conflicts, a nationalist hysteria over alleged threats is particularly prominent. The country plays a leading role in NATO’s war against Russia, and longstanding anti-Russian resentments have been systematically intensified since the beginning of the war. They go hand in hand with a military buildup supported across party lines. Socialism AI by the WSWS SocialismAI.com Questions about this article? Ask more questions at SocialismAI.com Military spending is rising year after year and currently stands at 4.8 percent of GDP, or around €48 billion. While Poland now maintains the largest land army in the EU, the role of the Territorial Defence Forces (WOT), Poland’s National Guard, has also been steadily expanded. Military education in schools, including firearms training, is intended to indoctrinate children in a militaristic spirit from an early age. As the army increasingly assumes police functions—as it does on the EU’s external border with Belarus—every soldier is portrayed as a national hero whose actions are considered beyond reproach, despite regular reports of human rights violations. When acclaimed director Agnieszka Holland denounced conditions at the border in her film Green Border (Zielona Granica) , she became the target of a campaign of vilification. Recent events have repeatedly demonstrated just how poisoned the political atmosphere has become. For example, Bartosz T. Wieliński, deputy editor-in-chief of Gazeta Wyborcza, made the absurd suggestion in a commentary that a “large-scale Russian operation to influence young people” was behind the violence in schools. The conflict over Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal between the government of Donald Tusk and PiS-aligned President Karol Nawrocki has also escalated in recent days. After Nawrocki refused to swear in newly elected constitutional judges chosen by parliament, and the court’s PiS-appointed president, Bogdan Święczkowski, denied them access to the court, Święczkowski was suspended and a female judge close to Tusk’s camp assumed temporary leadership of the court. Far-right extremists besieged the court, while Nawrocki cut short a foreign trip and gained access to the sealed-off court building after midnight. During the incident, the former amateur boxer became involved in a physical altercation with one of the newly appointed female judges.
